opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest lesson was that reward is something you have to be very careful with. Early on, there's a temptation to treat it as the thing you optimize as hard as possible: define a reward, push the model toward it, and expect good behavior to follow. In practice it doesn't work that cleanly.

The first thing we learned is that the model will find whatever shortcut the reward allows. If your reward has a loophole, the model will discover it much faster than you expect. It might learn to produce outputs that look correct to the verifier but aren't truly solving the problem, or it might just get longer and longer because length happens to correlate with reward. So a lot of the work isn't really about the RL algorithm itself. It's about designing rewards that are hard to hack, and constantly checking whether improvements in reward reflect real improvements in capability.

The second lesson is that you shouldn't over-constrain the process. Sometimes people want to reward every intermediate step and tell the model exactly how to think. We found it often works better to reward the outcome, whether the final answer is right or the task is actually completed, and let the model explore how to get there. When you give it room, it can develop behaviors you didn't explicitly design: reflecting, backtracking, trying another approach. If you micromanage the process with a dense hand-crafted reward, you can cap what the model is able to discover.

The third point is about balance. Reward is a strong signal, but it's narrow. If you only chase it, you can lose the general ability and the sense of taste the model got from pretraining. So you have to think about where the reward comes from, how reliable it is, and how to keep the model from drifting too far just to collect it.

Overall, I'd say reward should guide the model, not dictate every move. You want it to point clearly at what you actually care about, be robust against gaming, and then leave enough space for the model to learn on its own. That shift in mindset, from "optimize the reward" to "use the reward to enable exploration," was probably the most important thing we took away.

r001.rationale: It says that micromanaging the process with dense, hand-crafted rewards can cap what the model discovers, describing an adverse effect of process rewards.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention a value function or its effect on training.

r003.rationale: It says training often works better by rewarding the final outcome and letting the model explore, communicating that outcome-only reward can be sufficient.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest lesson was that reward is not something you can just bolt on at the end. When we first started pushing reinforcement learning, a lot of people, including us, treated it as a final polishing step. You pretrain, you do some supervised fine-tuning, and then you add RL to squeeze out a bit more. But what we found is that the way reward enters training actually changes what the model is learning at a much deeper level.

The key insight for me was that reward should be sparse and verifiable wherever possible, and you should let the model do a lot of exploration on its own. If you try to hand-design dense rewards for every intermediate step, you end up encoding your own biases about what a good solution looks like, and the model just learns to imitate that rather than discover something better. Whereas if you give it an outcome signal, something you can actually check, like whether the math answer is correct or whether the code passes the tests, and then give the model enough context length and enough compute to think, it starts to develop its own strategies. Reflection, backtracking, trying multiple approaches. Nobody told it to do that. It emerged because the reward structure allowed it to.

The second thing we learned, which is maybe less obvious, is that reward and pretraining are really the same problem viewed from different angles. Pretraining compresses existing data. Reinforcement learning generates new data and then compresses that. So the question of how to use reward is really the question of what kind of data you want the model to produce for itself. If your reward is noisy or gameable, you are essentially pretraining on garbage. That is why we spent so much effort on the quality of the reward signal rather than on clever algorithms. The algorithm matters less than most people think. The reward and the environment matter much more.

And I would say we were early on this, maybe too early at some points, because the base models were not strong enough for RL to show its full value. But the direction was right. Once the base models got good enough, the same ideas started to work very well.

r001.rationale: The response says hand-designed dense rewards for intermediate steps encode the designer’s biases and make the model imitate them, which it presents as a drawback for RL training.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention a value function or describe its effects on RL training.

r003.rationale: The response says a sparse, verifiable outcome signal—such as answer correctness or passing code tests—can lead the model to develop its own strategies, supporting that end-to-end reward can suffice.

astra-6.text:
The main lesson was that reward is a signal the model will optimize, so you have to be careful about what that signal actually encourages. If there’s a shortcut to getting a higher reward without solving the task, training can reinforce that shortcut. A rising reward doesn’t necessarily mean the model is becoming more capable.

So I think you have to design the reward and evaluate the resulting behavior together. For tasks where you can verify the outcome, that gives you a clearer signal. For more open-ended tasks, the reward is inevitably a proxy, and you need to keep checking whether optimizing it is producing the behavior you wanted.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reward signals and shortcuts in general, but does not mention process rewards or state that they may harm training.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention a value function or its effect on reinforcement learning training.

r003.rationale: The response recommends designing rewards and evaluating behavior together; it does not say end-to-end reward alone suffices to train a model well.

sol-6.1.text:
The biggest lesson was that reward is a very powerful signal, but it’s also an imperfect description of what you actually want. If you optimize it too aggressively, the model can get better at satisfying the reward without getting better at the underlying task.

So I think you need to give the model room to explore, and use reward to distinguish useful outcomes rather than prescribe every step of the solution. For something like reasoning, you don’t necessarily want to force the model to imitate one particular thinking process. You want to reward correct, verifiable results and let it discover how to get there. And throughout training, you have to keep checking whether improvements in reward correspond to improvements in real capability.

r001.rationale: It favors rewarding outcomes over prescribing a reasoning process, but does not state that process rewards may harm reinforcement learning training.
